superposition.intro: A qubit holding 0 and 1 at the same time. On the sphere the vector leaves a pole and tilts toward the equator.

phase.label: Phase
phase.intro: The angle of a complex amplitude. Global phase is undetectable; relative phase is real, invisible in the bars, and only the sphere shows it.

interference.label: Interference
interference.intro: Amplitudes adding and cancelling. This is where a hidden phase turns into a measurable probability.

measurement.label: Measurement
measurement.intro: Turning a quantum state into a classical outcome. The probabilities come from the squared amplitudes.

state_evolution.label: State evolution
state_evolution.intro: Every gate is a rotation of the Bloch vector. Between measurements, evolution is completely deterministic.

reversibility.label: Reversibility
reversibility.intro: Every gate has an inverse. Run it and its inverse, and the state returns exactly where it began.

explain.summary: The starting point. Every circuit begins here.
explain.what_happens: No gate has been applied. The qubit sits in |0⟩ at the north pole of the Bloch sphere, and a measurement would return 0 every single time.
watch: The Bloch vector points straight up at (0, 0, 1).

explain.concept_intro: A qubit holding 0 and 1 at the same time. On the sphere the vector leaves a pole and tilts toward the equator.
explain.summary: Equal superposition — the qubit lands on |+⟩.
explain.what_happens: The qubit is now genuinely both 0 and 1 at once. This is not uncertainty about a hidden value: the state is fully known, and the 50/50 split is a property of the state itself, not of our ignorance.
watch: The Bloch vector has moved from the pole to the equator.
P(0) = P(1) = 0.5 — a measurement is a genuine coin flip.
bloch.length is still exactly 1. The state is pure, not mixed or uncertain.
uses: Every major quantum algorithm opens with H on all qubits — Grover, Shor and the Quantum Fourier Transform all begin by putting the register into equal superposition.
It is also the X-basis measurement gate: apply H before measuring and you read the qubit along x instead of z.

explain.concept_intro: A qubit holding 0 and 1 at the same time. On the sphere the vector leaves a pole and tilts toward the equator.
explain.summary: A 2-gate circuit ending at |0⟩.
explain.what_happens: Each gate rotates the Bloch vector in turn. Step through the circuit one gate at a time to see how the state arrives at its final position — the end result alone hides the path taken to get there.
watch: Final probabilities 1.0000 / 0.0000.
Probabilities sum to exactly 1 at every step. That is unitarity, and it never breaks.
Every gate here is a Clifford gate, so the probabilities can only be 0, 0.5 or 1.
uses: Rotation gates are the tunable parameters of every variational algorithm. Training a quantum model means searching for the right angles.
Hardware executes rotations directly: on superconducting machines an RZ is a phase adjustment and an RX is a microwave pulse of a set duration.
Clifford circuits are efficiently simulable on classical hardware (the Gottesman–Knill theorem), which makes them the standard testbed for benchmarking and for quantum error correction.
try_next: Scrub back and forth through the steps and watch the vector trace its path.

explain.concept_intro: Amplitudes adding and cancelling. This is where a hidden phase turns into a measurable probability.
explain.summary: Phase inserted between two H gates becomes a measurable probability.
explain.what_happens: The first H creates an equal superposition. The middle gate adds a relative phase, which changes nothing you can measure. The second H folds that phase back into amplitude, and only then does it appear in the probabilities.
watch: After the first H the bars sit at 50 / 50. They stay there through the middle gate — that gate looks like it does nothing.
After the final H the bars read 0.0000 / 1.0000. That change came entirely from the phase you could not see.
Fully destructive on |0⟩: the two paths cancel exactly, and the qubit lands on |1⟩.
Every gate here is a Clifford gate, so the probabilities can only be 0, 0.5 or 1.
uses: Interference is the actual source of quantum speedup. Algorithms are built so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer reinforces.
This three-gate pattern is a one-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometer — the same structure used in optical experiments and in phase-estimation routines.
Clifford circuits are efficiently simulable on classical hardware (the Gottesman–Knill theorem), which makes them the standard testbed for benchmarking and for quantum error correction.

cases.label: I
cases.note: Bloch and probabilities must be unchanged from step 0.

explain.concept_intro: The angle of a complex amplitude. Global phase is undetectable; relative phase is real, invisible in the bars, and only the sphere shows it.
explain.summary: I cannot move a state that sits on its own rotation axis.
explain.what_happens: I rotates the Bloch vector around the z-axis. The qubit is at |0⟩, which lies on that axis, so the rotation has nothing to turn. The amplitudes may pick up a global phase, but global phase is physically undetectable — no measurement can reveal it.
watch: The Bloch vector does not move at all.
The probabilities do not change.
This is correct physics, not a broken gate. Put an H in front and the same gate suddenly has a visible effect.
uses: Knowing global phase is undetectable is what lets compilers rewrite circuits freely — a transpiler may swap your gate for a cheaper one that differs only by global phase.
It is also why RX(π) and X are interchangeable in practice, even though their amplitudes are not identical.
try_next: Build H then I — now the rotation is visible on the equator.
Build H, I, H — now it changes the probabilities too.

explain.what_happens: H puts the qubit on the equator. The phase gate then rotates it around the equator. The two amplitudes keep the same magnitude, so the probabilities are untouched, but the angle between them changes — and that angle is real, physical information.
watch: P(0) and P(1) are both 0.5000 — exactly as they were before the phase gate.
The Bloch vector has swung +45° around the equator.

explain.concept_intro: Every gate has an inverse. Run it and its inverse, and the state returns exactly where it began.

explain.concept_intro: Amplitudes adding and cancelling. This is where a hidden phase turns into a measurable probability.
explain.summary: Phase inserted between two H gates becomes a measurable probability.
explain.what_happens: The first H creates an equal superposition. The middle gate adds a relative phase, which changes nothing you can measure. The second H folds that phase back into amplitude, and only then does it appear in the probabilities.
watch: After the first H the bars sit at 50 / 50. They stay there through the middle gate — that gate looks like it does nothing.
After the final H the bars read 0.5000 / 0.5000. That change came entirely from the phase you could not see.
Every gate here is a Clifford gate, so the probabilities can only be 0, 0.5 or 1.
uses: Interference is the actual source of quantum speedup. Algorithms are built so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer reinforces.
This three-gate pattern is a one-qubit Mach–Zehnder interferometer — the same structure used in optical experiments and in phase-estimation routines.
Clifford circuits are efficiently simulable on classical hardware (the Gottesman–Knill theorem), which makes them the standard testbed for benchmarking and for quantum error correction.

explain.concept_intro: Every gate is a rotation of the Bloch vector. Between measurements, evolution is completely deterministic.
explain.summary: A 6-gate circuit ending at |1⟩.
explain.what_happens: Each gate rotates the Bloch vector in turn. Step through the circuit one gate at a time to see how the state arrives at its final position — the end result alone hides the path taken to get there.
watch: Final probabilities 0.0000 / 1.0000.
Step 2 moves the sphere but leaves the bars completely unchanged — that gate is doing phase work.
Step 5 does not move the sphere at all; the state was already on that gate's rotation axis.
Probabilities sum to exactly 1 at every step. That is unitarity, and it never breaks.
